newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW-Shake-out seen in French online business.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Shake-out seen in French online business.

text.p: This year will see a ruthless round of concentration in the French online business with only a few big players with links to telecoms companies surviving out of the six active now, Herve Digne, managing director of multimedia publishers Hachette Filipacchi Grolier said.
Digne said in an interview on Monday that it would take until at least 2005 before publishers could make real money on the Internet.

"The market is currently fragmented between five or six access providers with some 20,000 subscribers each. Because there is a price war in the sector, these activities on their own are not very profitable," Digne said.
"I believe that there is going to be a restructuring around companies that have a link with a telecoms operator," he said.

In France, Wanadoo has a link with France Telecom, Microsoft's MSN has a priviliged deal with the same operator while Generale des Eaux Cegetel telecoms unit has the ambition to become an access provider.
EasyNet is related to British Telecom but others such as AOL, Infonie, Calvacom or Club Internet do not.
"If the market continues to grow as slowly as it does now, not all of them can survive and will have to restructure," Digne said.
Meanwhile, Club Internet is the priviliged partner for HFG, both being part of Lagardere Groupe.
HFG has published a series of CD-ROMS and manages eight web sites related to the big magazine titles of the group, in particular Elle but also Paris Match.
Digne said that the eight sites managed by HFG attracted 1.2 million page visits per month and the group was pricing adverts for the pages at 250 francs per thousand visits.
A ninth site, for cinema magazine ParisScope, will be launched soon with a special search feature for users to select which film to see the same evening.

Digne said that at the moment there were between 5,000 and 7,000 French web sites and while this number was set to increase he believed that there would be only a limited number of sites which would be visited frequently.
"Firstly, not many publishers update their pages regularly and secondly there is the psuh development," he said.
"Push" on the Internet is a word used to describe programmes and services which deliver information to a person instead of the reader having to look for it.

Elle will be available as a "button" on Microsoft Explorer 4.0, articles can be sent as mail to Netscape users and HFG is in talks with BackWeb, an Israeli company which has developed a content delivery technology, to "bring" its content and adverts to readers over the Internet.
BackWeb was founded in 1995 by BRM Technologies Inc and operates in a market estimated by researchers the Yankee Group at $4.6 billion by the year 2000.

Digne said Elle would further develop its local content and make a central international site of the English language Elle.com site, with such added value services as picture reports on fashion shows within half an hour after they were staged.
HFG will also shortly sign a deal with a cosmetics company for both international and local advertising on the Elle pages on the Internet.
But Digne refuses to be carried away by forecasts of spectacular growth in the internet that would make advertisement a big source of revenue.

"I don't think that any company will be able to make a real return on investment until the year 2005. In the meantime editors like us will have to try to limit the losses and get to know the new techniques to adapt to the new market," he said.

In CD-ROM, Digne said that there were signs that many multimedia computers had been sold for Christmas and that CD-ROM sales could rise. But he noted that there had been 1,500 new titles launched in the European market last year and many publishers were still waiting to reach break-even.
"If a CD-Rom title would sell 10,000 copies it's a best seller. The break-even lies often around 6,000 copies and many titles are far from that," he said.
